name: Freya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the under-shepherd at Brackenridge, a hill farm with about eleven hundred ewes spread over the hill and the common grazing above it. Right now the tups, the rams, are in with the ewes, so every morning I'm out on the quad bike with my two dogs, Moss and Tib, checking who's been marked and who's stuck in a ditch. Afternoons it's fencing, feeding hay to the ones down in the in-bye fields near the house, and listening to Ewan tell me I did it wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the hill on a clear frosty morning, when the dogs bring a whole face of sheep down and it's like water pouring off the slope. What wears me out is the weather and the money, mostly the money. A good lamb pays less than it did when Ewan started, and every year he says this might be the last year he runs the hill.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He owns it, he's sixty-four, and his kids live in the city and don't want it. I've been with him three years. I came late to sheep, I worked in a garden centre before, so I'm still the slow one at lambing, still pulling the wrong leg sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it might save me an hour on the paperwork. I'd probably post something about it being handy, nothing dramatic. Most people up here would just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd use it for the movement forms, the records of every sheep we move off the farm, which I hate. I already ask one of those AI chat things to word emails to the auction mart sometimes. A bit better and it's a bit more useful, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, and maybe finally do the sheep scanning course in February. Put a bit more away. Sam and I want a dog of our own that isn't a working dog, which sounds silly but it's the dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly pleased, if it means less time at the kitchen table with forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the AI chat now and then. What was the last thing you asked it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to tell the difference between a lame ewe with scald and one with foot rot. I didn't trust it fully, so I asked Ewan too, and he said the computer was right, which annoyed him. That's about my level, check it, then check with a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the money side you'd change, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a fair price for lamb, that's all. Last autumn our best lambs made less at the mart than the year before, and the feed went up. Ewan says it's been like that his whole life, which isn't much comfort.

S0.say: I'd say good, it might save me an hour on paperwork, and post that it's handy. Most people up here would just shrug at it.
S0.think: I'd use it for the movement forms I hate, and I already ask an AI chat to word emails to the auction mart. A bit better just means a bit more useful.
S0.do: Carries on as now and books the sheep scanning course for February. Saves a little more each month with her partner Sam.
S0.feel: Calm, and slightly pleased at less time spent on forms.
S0.quote: That's about my level, check it, then check with a person.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is practical about AI: she uses it, double-checks it, and isn't impressed or scared. The farm's real threat in her mind is the price of lamb and Ewan retiring. She was cheerful, and the dog dream made her laugh at herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not new up here, farms stopped hiring beginners years ago because they can't afford them. I got in because Ewan was desperate. I'd say that online and people would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it really means for me is Brackenridge doesn't get a second under-shepherd after me, and when Ewan goes, there's nobody to train. Fewer beginners means I'm the last one who learned from someone like him. That's sad more than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to learn faster, every job Ewan does, while he's still here. Lambing, the dipping, how he reads the hill. I'd write it all down in a notebook, actually, or record him talking on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my job, more for the whole way of doing it fading out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Recording Ewan. Would he let you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then he'd talk for an hour. He told me last month which corner of the top hill the ewes shelter in when the wind is from the east, and I'd never have worked that out in ten years. No machine is going to know that unless someone tells it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's to blame for farms not hiring beginners, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The prices, mostly, and whoever sets them, the supermarkets and the big meat buyers. Small hill farms run on almost nothing. I don't blame Ewan, he paid me before he paid himself some months.

S1.say: I'd say farms stopped hiring beginners years ago because they couldn't afford them. I only got in because Ewan was desperate, and people up here would agree.
S1.think: I think Brackenridge won't get another under-shepherd after me. I might be the last one who learned from someone like Ewan, which is sad more than scary.
S1.do: Learns every job Ewan does while he's still working, from lambing to dipping. Records him talking on her phone and keeps a notebook of how he reads the hill.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mainly about a whole way of working fading out.
S1.quote: Fewer beginners means I'm the last one who learned from someone like him.
S1.fieldNote: She sees the loss as knowledge, not jobs. The story about east-wind shelter was vivid and she clearly treasures what Ewan knows. Her steady, wait-and-see nature shows: she plans to learn more, not to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office layoffs are awful and the government should step in, with real support, not a leaflet. I'd share things from the farmers' union and the teachers' union, because Sam would be worried too. I'd be angry online, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think about Sam more than me. Teachers aren't office workers exactly, but the school office would go, and the council that pays her. On the hill, nothing changes, the sheep don't care who does the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Sam and work out what we'd do if her hours were cut. We have about three months saved, so I'd stop the little extras, the takeaway on Fridays. I'd also ask Ewan about the forms and records, because if the AI can do them properly, I'll happily hand them over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for Sam, oddly relieved for me, and then guilty about the relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut after the Friday takeaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership I don't use, honestly, the hill is my gym. Then the second car, which would be hard because Sam's school is twenty minutes away. I'd try to keep the dog fund, that one's not negotiable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some new AI jobs appear in this picture. Would any of them tempt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not if it means a desk in a city. Maybe if one of them was about farms, like helping farmers with the records, I'd look. But I'd want to see someone else do it first and not get burned.

S2.say: I'd say the office layoffs are awful and the government should give real support, not a leaflet. I'd share posts from the farmers' and teachers' unions and be a bit angry online.
S2.think: I'd worry about Sam more than myself, because her school office and the council could be cut. On the hill nothing changes, since sheep don't care who does the payroll.
S2.do: Plans with Sam for cut hours, using their three months of savings, and drops the Friday takeaway and unused gym membership. Asks Ewan to hand the farm forms to an AI tool if it works properly.
S2.feel: Worried for Sam, relieved for herself, then guilty about the relief.
S2.quote: On the hill, nothing changes, the sheep don't care who does the payroll.
S2.fieldNote: Her worry is all about her partner. She'd hand the paperwork to AI without regret, which fits her steady attitude: happy to use what works. The dog fund came back as a joke, but she meant it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if the city people are booming on shares and houses while people lose jobs, tax them and pay for rural services. Bus routes, the vet, the mobile phone signal. I'd go to a protest if there was one in the county town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the hill is probably the safest place in the country in this picture. But we rent our cottage from the estate next door, and if house prices boom, people from the city buy the cottages for weekends. Then there's nowhere for shepherds to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ewan if there's any chance of the cottage at Brackenridge, the one his mother lived in. I'd keep saving and maybe look into one of those shared ownership schemes, if the council does them out here. And I'd stay put at the farm, because a physical job is the thing to hold onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. The work is safe, the life around it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has that happened already, cottages going to weekend people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three on our road in two years. The one next door has a hot tub and the lights are on maybe six weekends a year. The old man who lived there did the hedges for the whole valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave sheep for something else in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had nowhere to live. The job's not the problem here, the roof is. If it came to it, I'd rather move to a worse farm with a cottage than a better one without.

S3.say: I'd say tax the people booming on shares and houses and spend it on rural services like buses, the vet and phone signal. I'd go to a protest in the county town.
S3.think: I think the hill is about the safest place to be, but booming house prices mean city people buy cottages for weekends. Then there's nowhere left for shepherds to live.
S3.do: Asks Ewan about the empty cottage at Brackenridge and looks into council shared ownership schemes. Keeps saving and stays firmly in her physical job.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the work is safe but the life around it isn't.
S3.quote: The one next door has a hot tub and the lights are on maybe six weekends a year.
S3.fieldNote: She frames the threat as housing and community, not her job. The hot tub detail was bitter but funny. She's clear that holding a hands-on job is the right move here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no robot that can do a hill in a snowstorm, and I'd mean it, publicly. But I'd also say the government needs to plan for farm workers this time, not leave us till last like always. I'd want the union to have a plan before the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less sure than I sound. There are already drones that move sheep, and collars that keep cows in a field without fences. If Ewan retires and the hill gets sold, a big company might run it with drones and one person in a van, and that person wouldn't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence in the first year, if it was proven to work on sheep. Not before, I'm not paying for a toy. I'd also talk to the other two hill farms in the valley about whether they'd share a shepherd, so there's work for me even if Brackenridge changes hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of fight in it. I don't want to be the person who stood on the hill saying it can't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ewan say if you told him you wanted to do a drone licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say over my dead body, then ask me to show him the video. He's like that, he hates new things for about a week. Then he wants to know exactly how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the day a drone brings the sheep down instead of Moss and Tib. What would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably stand at the gate and cry a bit, honestly. Then I'd want to see if it missed any, because the dogs never do. If it did a clean job, I'd have to accept it, but I'd keep the dogs whatever happens.

S4.say: I'd say publicly that no robot can work a hill in a snowstorm. I'd also say the government and the union must plan for farm workers before the machines arrive.
S4.think: I'm less sure than I sound, because drones that move sheep already exist. If the hill is sold, a company could run it with drones and one person in a van, and that wouldn't be me.
S4.do: Takes a drone licence in the first year, once it's proven to work with sheep. Talks to the two other hill farms in the valley about sharing a shepherd so she has work if Brackenridge is sold.
S4.feel: Anxious, with some fight in it.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the person who stood on the hill saying it can't happen.
S4.fieldNote: Clear gap between say and think: in public the hill is robot-proof, in private she knows drones already herd sheep. Her plan is cautious but real, and waits for proof. Ewan's reaction, hating something for a week then wanting to learn it, sounds a lot like her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because it's the only one that reaches the hill. What would help is support for small farms to share the new kit, so it's not just big companies with drones. And a proper scheme so shepherds can live where they work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the dogs. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a drone moves the sheep, what happens to the dogs and the people who breed them? Moss is the best thing in my life after Sam, and I'm not joking.

headlineQuote: On the hill, nothing changes, the sheep don't care who does the payroll.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old under-shepherd on a hill farm with about 1,100 ewes, three years into the job after working in a garden centre. She uses AI chat tools now and then but always checks with a person, and her left-leaning views come out as anger about rural services and housing. In the first three pictures she worries most about her partner Sam's job and about weekend homes emptying her valley. The robot picture worries her more than she admits in public: she knows drones already move sheep, and plans to learn them once they're proven.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because it's the only one that reaches the hill and a sold farm could be run with drones.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small farms to share new equipment so it isn't only big companies, and a scheme so shepherds can afford to live where they work.
